title: Minimum Number of Operations to Sort a Binary Tree by Level
statement:
You are given the `root` of a binary tree in which no two nodes hold the same value. A level is the set of nodes at the same distance (number of edges) from the root, read from left to right.

One operation picks two nodes that lie on the same level and exchanges their values. Return the fewest operations needed so that, on every level, the values read from left to right are strictly increasing.
constraints: The tree has between 1 and 10^5 nodes
notes:
## Intuition

Swaps never move a value to another level, so every level is an independent puzzle: given a row of distinct numbers, what is the fewest swaps that sorts it? Compare the row with its sorted copy. Each value has exactly one correct position, so following "where should this value go" from position to position traces cycles. A cycle of length k needs exactly k - 1 swaps, and each swap that drops a value into its correct place achieves that. A breadth-first traversal hands us the rows one level at a time.

## Approach

1. Keep a running total `swaps` and start `queue` with the root.
2. For each level, copy the node values into `values` (left to right) and gather the children into `next`.
3. Sort a copy into `sorted` and record in `target` the index each value belongs at.
4. Walk `i` across `values`. While the value at `i` is not where it belongs, swap it to its index `j` and count one swap; each swap fixes one value for good.
5. Move to `next`. When no level is left, return `swaps`.

## Example 1, step by step

`root = [1,4,3,7,6,8,5,null,null,null,null,9,null,10]`. Level `[1]` is sorted. Level `[4,3]`: `4` belongs at index 1, one swap gives `[3,4]`. Level `[7,6,8,5]` sorts to `[5,6,7,8]`: `7` goes to index 2 giving `[8,6,7,5]`, then `8` goes to index 3 giving `[5,6,7,8]`: two swaps. Level `[9,10]` is sorted. Total `swaps = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): each level is sorted once and each swap places one value permanently.
- Space: O(w) for the queue, `values`, `sorted` and `target`, where w is the widest level.

## Pitfalls

- Swaps only happen inside a level, so do not sort the whole tree's values together.
- Advance `i` only after its slot holds the right value; a single swap per index can leave a misplaced value behind.
- Sort numbers with a comparator: the default `sort()` compares them as strings.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `swaps` | operations counted so far over all levels |
| `queue`, `next` | nodes of the current level and of the level below |
| `values` | the current level's values, swapped in place as we count |
| `sorted` | the same values in increasing order |
| `target` | maps each value to the index it must end up at |
| `i`, `j` | the slot being fixed and the slot its value belongs in |
